entry:
Social unit of people sharing one or more socially significant characteristics, such as place, norms, [[Culture|culture]], [[Religion|religion]], values, customs, or [[Identity (social science)|identity]]. Communities may share a sense of place within a geographical area, such as a [[Country|country]], village, town, or neighborhood, or may exist in virtual space through communication platforms. Durable good relations that extend beyond immediate genealogical ties also define a sense of community, which is important to people's identity and to roles in social institutions such as family, work, government, and society. Communities are usually small relative to personal social ties, but the word may also refer to national, international, and virtual communities.

The English word derives from the Old French *comuneté*, which comes from the [[Latin]] *communitas*, 'community' or 'public spirit'.

Disciplines use the term differently. In [[Archaeology|archaeology]] it means either an ancient settlement or a group of people living near one another who interacted socially; archaeologists infer communities from similarities in material culture, from house types to pottery styles. In [[Ecology|ecology]] a community is an assemblage of populations, potentially of different species, interacting through competition, predation, and mutualism. Major communities, such as a forest or a lake, are self-sustaining; minor communities, such as fungi decomposing a log, rely on others. Early sociological studies treated communities as fringe groups at the behest of local power elites. The word usually carries a positive connotation, which politicians and advertisers exploit rhetorically.

Instrument showing the [[Cardinal direction|cardinal directions]], used for [[Navigation|navigation]] and geographic orientation. It typically consists of a magnetized needle, or another element such as a compass card, that pivots to align itself with magnetic north. Compasses often show angles in degrees: north is 0°, east 90°, south 180°, and west 270°.

The magnetic compass works because the needle aligns itself with the horizontal component of [[Earth's magnetic field]], which exerts a torque on it, pulling its north end approximately toward Earth's North magnetic pole. The needle turns on a low-friction pivot, in better compasses a jewel bearing, and settles after a few seconds. Magnetic north differs from true north by an angle called magnetic declination, which varies with location and changes slowly over time, so maps usually give the local value. Modern compasses commonly seal the needle in a liquid-filled capsule, which damps oscillation.

One of the earliest known references to the magnetic properties of lodestone was made by the 6th-century BC Greek philosopher [[Thales of Miletus]]. The magnetic compass was first invented in China as a device for divination, as early as the [[Han dynasty]] (since c. 206 BC). The first compasses used for navigation appeared in China by 1088 during the [[Song dynasty]], as described by [[Shen Kuo]]; they used iron needles magnetized by striking them with a lodestone. The first recorded use in [[Western Europe]] occurred around 1190 and in the Islamic world in the 13th century. Dry compasses appeared around 1300, and the liquid-filled compass supplanted them in the early 20th century.

Number of the form a + bi, where a and b are [[Real number|real numbers]] and i is the [[Imaginary unit|imaginary unit]], satisfying i² = −1. The number a is the real part and b the imaginary part. The set of complex numbers is denoted ℂ.

Complex numbers extend the real numbers and support addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division under the same associative, commutative, and distributive laws, which makes them a [[Field (mathematics)|field]]. They are added by adding real and imaginary parts separately, and multiplied using the distributive law and i² = −1: (a + bi)(c + di) = (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i. In electromagnetism and electrical engineering, j is often written instead of i, because i commonly denotes electric current.

Each complex number corresponds to a point (a, b) in the complex plane, or Argand diagram, with the real part on the horizontal axis. Addition then corresponds to translation of the plane, and multiplication to scaling and rotation. Complex numbers give solutions to all non-constant polynomial equations, a result known as the [[Fundamental theorem of algebra]].

Because the square of any nonzero real number is positive, square roots of negative numbers were historically considered impossible. In the 16th century such roots proved helpful in solving [[Cubic equation|cubic equations]]; [[Gerolamo Cardano]] encountered them while deriving formulas for these equations, though he regarded them with suspicion. They were named imaginary numbers in the 17th century. Acceptance grew through the work of [[Leonhard Euler]] and later [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]]. Complex numbers model waves and quantum states in physics and are used in analyzing alternating-current circuits, signal processing, and fluid dynamics.

Machine that can be programmed to carry out sequences of arithmetic or logical operations automatically. Modern digital electronic computers perform sets of operations known as programs, which enable a wide range of tasks. Numbering only a few in the 1930s, computers are now ubiquitous, from single-purpose devices such as microwave ovens and remote controls to personal computers, smartphones, and supercomputers. They power the [[Internet]], which links billions of computers and users.

A modern computer consists of at least one processing element, typically a [[Central processing unit|central processing unit]] in the form of a microprocessor, together with memory, typically semiconductor chips. The processing element carries out arithmetic and logical operations, and a control unit can change the order of operations in response to stored information. Peripheral devices include input devices such as keyboards, output devices such as monitors, and devices such as touchscreens that do both.

The word first meant a person who performed calculations; the *Oxford English Dictionary* records this use in 1613, and by 1943 most human computers were women. The [[Abacus|abacus]] has aided calculation since ancient times; the Roman abacus developed from devices used in Babylonia as early as 2400 BCE. The [[Antikythera mechanism]], discovered in 1901 and dated to c. 100 BCE, is believed to be the earliest known mechanical analog computer. Early digital electronic calculating machines were developed during World War II. Successive technologies, from electromechanical parts and thermionic valves to the [[Transistor|transistor]] and the [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuit]], produced smaller and more efficient designs, leading to the microprocessor and the microcomputer revolution of the 1970s. [[Moore's law]] noted that transistor counts doubled every two years.

Study of computation, information, and automation and their associated phenomena. It spans theoretical disciplines, such as algorithms, the theory of computation, and information theory, and applied disciplines, including the design and implementation of hardware and software. Its fundamental concern is determining what can and cannot be automated, and the Turing Award is generally recognized as its highest distinction.

Algorithms and data structures are central to the field. The theory of computation concerns abstract models of computation and the classes of problems they can solve. [[Cryptography]] and computer security study secure communication and the prevention of vulnerabilities. Human–computer interaction examines the interfaces between people and machines, and software engineering the principles of developing software. [[Artificial intelligence]] and machine learning aim to synthesize processes such as problem-solving, decision-making, and learning found in humans and animals.

The foundations predate the digital computer. Wilhelm Schickard built the first working mechanical calculator in 1623, and in 1673 Gottfried Leibniz demonstrated the Stepped Reckoner. [[Charles Babbage]] began designing the Difference Engine in 1822 and the programmable Analytical Engine in 1834, adopting punched cards derived from the Jacquard loom. In 1843 [[Ada Lovelace]] wrote, in notes to a translated article on the Analytical Engine, an algorithm to compute the Bernoulli numbers, considered the first published algorithm tailored for a computer. In 1936 [[Alan Turing]] introduced the universal Turing machine, formalizing the principles of computation. During the 1940s machines such as the Atanasoff–Berry computer and ENIAC led the word computer to refer to machines rather than people, and the field broadened to study computation in general.

[[Composite material]] of aggregate bound together with a fluid cement that cures to a solid. It is the most widely used building material and the most-manufactured material in the world; only water is used more. Cement-bound concrete differs from the less rigid, less durable asphaltic concrete, which has a bituminous binder.

When aggregate is mixed with dry Portland [[Cement|cement]] and water, the mixture forms a fluid slurry that can be poured and molded. The cement reacts with the water in an exothermic process called hydration, which hardens it over several hours into a durable, stone-like matrix. Most structural concrete is poured with embedded [[Steel|steel]] rebar to provide tensile strength, yielding reinforced concrete. Non-cementitious types include asphalt concrete, with a [[Bitumen|bitumen]] binder frequently used for road surfaces, and polymer concretes.

The word comes from the Latin *concretus*, 'compact' or 'condensed'. Concrete floors were found in the royal palace of Tiryns, Greece, dated roughly to 1400–1200 BC, and the Assyrian Jerwan Aqueduct (688 BC) used waterproof concrete. The Romans used concrete extensively from 300 BC to AD 476, making it from quicklime, pozzolana, and an aggregate of pumice. It freed Roman builders from the limits of stone and brick, and the [[Colosseum]] was built largely of it; the Pantheon has the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome. Modern tests show Roman concrete had a compressive strength similar to modern Portland-cement concrete, c. 20 MPa, but a far lower tensile strength. Its durability is attributed to volcanic rock and ash in the mix, and it resists seawater erosion better than modern concrete.

System of thought and behavior originating in ancient China, variously described as a tradition, philosophy, religion, theory of government, or way of life. Also called Ruism, it was founded by [[Confucius]] in the Hundred Schools of Thought era (c. 500 BCE) and integrates philosophy, ethics, and social governance, with a core focus on virtue, social harmony, and familial responsibility.

Confucianism emphasizes virtue through self-cultivation and communal effort. Key virtues include *rén* (benevolence), *yì* (righteousness), *lǐ* (propriety), *zhì* (wisdom), and *xìn* (sincerity). These are tied to *tiān* (Heaven), which, though not an omnipotent deity, is upheld as a transcendent moral order. Tradition holds that he authored or edited the Five Classics, though scholars debate how far they took shape in his hands. His sayings are preserved in the [[Analects]].

Suppressed under the Legalist [[Qin dynasty]] (c. 200 BCE), Confucianism flourished under the [[Han dynasty]] (c. 130 BCE), becoming the dominant ideological framework. Under the Tang dynasty (c. 600 CE), in response to the rising influence of [[Buddhism]] and [[Taoism]], Neo-Confucianism developed; it became central to the imperial examination system and the scholar-official class of the [[Song dynasty]]. The abolition of the examination system in 1905 marked the decline of state-endorsed Confucianism. In the early 20th century Chinese reformers associated it with China's Century of Humiliation and embraced other ideologies, including Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles of the People and later Maoism. Critics argue that it can entrench hierarchy and authority; others credit it with fostering social cohesion and East Asian economic development. It remains influential in China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam, and Chinese diaspora communities.

Chinese philosopher of the [[Spring and Autumn period]], traditionally considered the paragon of Chinese sages. Born Kong Qiu, he is known in Mandarin as Kongzi, 'Master Kong'; the Latinized name was coined in the late 16th century by Jesuit missionaries. His teachings, called [[Confucianism]], emphasized personal and governmental morality, harmonious social relationships, righteousness, kindness, sincerity, and a ruler's responsibility to lead by virtue.

According to tradition he was born in Zou, in modern Qufu, [[Shandong]], in the state of Lu. His father, an elderly commandant of the local garrison, died when Confucius was three, and his mother raised him in poverty. He married at 19. In 501 BCE he was appointed governor of a town and eventually rose to Minister of Crime.

Confucius considered himself a transmitter of the values of earlier periods, which he claimed had been abandoned in his time. He advocated filial piety, endorsing strong family loyalty, ancestor veneration, and respect for elders. He championed the Silver Rule, a negative form of the [[Golden Rule]]: 'Do not do unto others what you do not want done to yourself.'

His ideas gained prominence during the [[Warring States period]] but suffered a setback after the Qin conquest. Under [[Emperor Wu of Han]] they received official sanction, and affiliated works became mandatory reading for careers in officialdom. Tradition credits him with authoring or editing the Five Classics, but modern scholars are cautious about attributing specific assertions to him, since some of the texts and philosophy were of older origin. Aphorisms of his teaching were compiled in the [[Analects]] many years after his death.

Awareness of something internal to oneself or of states or objects in one's external environment. It has been the topic of debate among philosophers, scientists, and theologians for millennia. There is no consensus on what exactly needs to be studied, or whether consciousness can be considered a scientific concept. In some accounts it is synonymous with [[Mind|mind]]; in others it is an aspect of it. Medicine also uses a definition that distinguishes [[Coma|coma]] from other states.

The English words date to the 17th century and derive from the Latin *conscius*, 'knowing with', especially in sharing a secret. [[Thomas Hobbes]] wrote in 1651 that when two or more people know the same fact, they are said to be conscious of it to one another. [[René Descartes]] is generally taken as the first philosopher to use the Latin *conscientia* in a sense closer to modern 'conscience', and the modern concept of consciousness is often attributed to [[John Locke]], who in 1690 defined it as 'the perception of what passes in a man's own mind'.

Philosophers frame the central question as the hard problem: why and how physical processes in the brain give rise to subjective experience. Distinctions are drawn between phenomenal experience, the 'what it is like' quality of feeling, and access consciousness, the availability of information for reporting and decision-making. In [[Neuroscience|neuroscience]], research seeks the neural correlates of consciousness. Prominent theories include higher-order theories, global neuronal workspace theory, predictive processing theories, and integrated information theory, which quantifies consciousness as irreducible causal integration. Whether it can arise in artificial systems remains debated.

Cultural, social, and political philosophy and ideology that seeks to promote and preserve traditional institutions, customs, and values. Its central tenets vary with the culture and civilization in which it appears. In Western culture, depending on nation and period, conservatives have sought to preserve institutions such as the nuclear family, organized religion, the military, the nation-state, constitutions, property rights, the rule of law, aristocracy, and [[Monarchy|monarchy]].

[[Edmund Burke]], an 18th-century Anglo-Irish statesman who opposed the [[French Revolution]], is credited as one of the forefathers of Western conservative thought in the 1790s, along with Joseph de Maistre. The first established political use of the term came in 1818 with François-René de Chateaubriand, during the Bourbon Restoration. Conservatism is counted among the three major ideologies with [[Liberalism|liberalism]] and [[Socialism|socialism]], and it is the dominant ideology in many countries, including Hungary, India, Iran, Israel, Italy, Japan, Poland, and Russia. Historically associated with [[Right-wing politics|right-wing politics]], it has been libertarian or authoritarian, populist or elitist, progressive or reactionary, moderate or extreme, and conservatives in different countries may disagree on a wide range of issues.

Scholars have tried to define it by principles. Andrew Heywood identifies five central beliefs: tradition, human imperfection, organic society, authority and hierarchy, and property. Russell Kirk, in *The Conservative Mind* (1953), set out five canons, including belief in a transcendent order, faith in custom and prescription, and respect for prudence. Samuel P. Huntington described conservatism as a situational ideology that defends the established institutions of its time. Left-wing theorists such as Corey Robin instead define it mainly as a defense of social and economic inequality, while supporters stress its caution toward utopian schemes.
